lessons.title: Distinct objects, factorials and position restrictions
lessons.summary: Choose an ordered sample space, then handle leading zeroes, blocks, distances and relative order without double-counting.
lessons.objective: Choose an ordered sample space, then handle leading zeroes, blocks, distances and relative order without double-counting.
lessons.before: Work with exact integer counts and identify what makes two outcomes different. Probability applications also use the conditional sample space from the preceding chapter. All arrangements here are in a line or in labelled rows; circular arrangements are excluded.
lessons.ideas:
The product rule counts a staged construction

Multiply the number of choices at each stage when each permitted partial construction has the stated number of continuations. Add disjoint cases when that number depends on an earlier choice. Mutually exclusive cases are not multiplied together.

Factorials and ordered selections

For non-negative integers, n! multiplies 1 through n, with 0!=1. For r distinct objects chosen and placed in order from n distinct objects,

\[{}^nP_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!},\qquad0\le r\le n.\]

Without repetition, the choices decrease after each position. If repetitions are allowed, the same count may remain available.

Leading zero and end conditions interact

A number cannot start with zero. For an even number with distinct digits, split the last digit into zero and non-zero even cases: they leave different numbers of non-zero first choices.

Blocks, exact separation and relative order

For two named objects together, treat them as one unit, arrange the units and restore their two internal orders. For exactly g objects between them, their positions differ by g+1. A relative order such as A before B is not an adjacency requirement.
lessons.method:
1. Decide whether order, object identity and group labels matter.
  2. Choose a disjoint case split or a staged construction.
  3. Count each allowed outcome once and restore internal orders if needed.
  4. Check restrictions, impossible cases and any overcounting factor.
  5. For a probability, use the same kind of equally likely outcome in numerator and denominator.
mistakes: Do not use combinations when the order matters.
Handle zero separately when forming numbers.
A block has internal orders only for distinguishable members.
Exactly g objects between two names differs from a minimum gap.

examples.title: A choice and an ordered programme differ
examples.question: Three of six different talks are selected. How many selections are possible, and how many ordered three-talk programmes?
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\text{selections}&=\binom63=20,\\\text{programmes}&=6\times5\times4=120.\end{aligned}\]

Each selection gives 3!=6 different programmes. Selecting a set does not assign its order.

examples.title: An even last digit changes the first choices
examples.question: Form a four-digit number from 0 to 5 without repeating a digit. Count all such numbers and the even ones.
examples.solution:
There are five non-zero first choices, then five, four and three choices.

\[5\times5\times4\times3=300.\]

For even numbers split on the final digit.

\[\begin{aligned}\text{last }0&:5\times4\times3=60,\\\text{last }2\text{ or }4&:2\times4\times4\times3=96.\end{aligned}\]

The even count is 156. Using five first choices in the second case would reuse its non-zero final digit.

examples.title: A named pair is a block with two orders
examples.question: Six different people, including A and B, stand in a line. Find the counts with A and B adjacent and with them apart.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\text{adjacent}&=2(5!)=240,\\\text{apart}&=6!-240=480.\end{aligned}\]

The five units are the pair-block and the four other people. The factor 2 restores AB and BA.

examples.title: Relative order does not require consecutive places
examples.question: Six different objects include A, B and C. How many linear orders have A before B before C?
examples.solution:
Every choice of their three positions has exactly one allowed order of A, B, C. Fill the other three positions freely.

\[\binom63\,3!=120.\]

Equivalently, one of the \(3!\) equally frequent relative orders is allowed, so the count is \(\frac{6!}{3!}\).

lessons.title: Repeated symbols, blocks and gap methods
lessons.summary: Count distinct visible patterns and use gaps to separate identical objects or enforce exactly one adjacent pair.
lessons.objective: Count distinct visible patterns and use gaps to separate identical objects or enforce exactly one adjacent pair.
lessons.before: Work with exact integer counts and identify what makes two outcomes different. Probability applications also use the conditional sample space from the preceding chapter. All arrangements here are in a line or in labelled rows; circular arrangements are excluded.
lessons.ideas:
Identical symbols do not acquire hidden labels

If n symbols have repeated multiplicities a,b,…, the number of distinct full patterns is

\[\frac{n!}{a!b!\cdots}.\]

Swapping two identical A tiles does not create a new pattern. Physical tile selections may require a different model; the final lesson makes that distinction explicit.

Apply restrictions after deciding what is identical

If an A must be first, remove one A and recount the remaining multiplicities. A block AA has only one internal pattern; a block AB of distinct symbols has two if either order is allowed.

Arrange the ordinary objects, then choose gaps

n distinct ordinary objects leave n+1 gaps, including both ends. Place at most one identical special object in each chosen gap to prevent adjacency. If the ends must be ordinary, use only the n−1 internal gaps.

Exactly one adjacent pair is a separate event

With three identical red counters, a pair and a single red must occupy distinct gaps of the ordinary objects. Their gap roles differ, even though the red counters do not. Do not include a triple or count the same pair twice. If two pair-events overlap, remove their common arrangements with the correct multiplicity.
lessons.method:
1. Decide whether order, object identity and group labels matter.
  2. Choose a disjoint case split or a staged construction.
  3. Count each allowed outcome once and restore internal orders if needed.
  4. Check restrictions, impossible cases and any overcounting factor.
  5. For a probability, use the same kind of equally likely outcome in numerator and denominator.
mistakes: Do not label identical tiles and then forget to remove overcounting.
Remove a fixed symbol before applying the repeated-factor denominator.
The end gaps count unless the ends are restricted.
Exactly one adjacent pair excludes both no pair and a triple.

examples.title: Fix a repeated symbol, then recount
examples.question: Arrange A,A,A,B,B,C in a line. Count all distinct patterns and those beginning with A.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\text{all}&=\frac{6!}{3!2!}=60,\\\text{first A}&=\frac{5!}{2!2!}=30.\end{aligned}\]

After fixing the first A, two As remain. Dividing the remaining patterns by 3! would remove too many orders.

examples.title: Two pair-events overlap
examples.question: Arrange A,A,B,B,C,D. Find the counts with both AA and BB together, with exactly one pair together, and the latter probability given at least one pair is together in a uniform random pattern.
examples.solution:
AA together gives \(\frac{5!}{2!}=60\); BB together also gives 60. Both together gives \(4!=24\). Let E mean exactly one pair together and H mean at least one pair together.

\[\begin{aligned}N(E)&=60+60-2(24)\\&=72,\\N(H)&=60+60-24=96,\\\mathrm P(E\mid H)&=\frac{72}{96}=\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}\]

examples.title: Separate two identical counters with ordinary objects
examples.question: Arrange four different numbered counters and two identical red counters. Count arrangements with the reds separated and with the reds adjacent.
examples.solution:
Arrange the numbered counters in \(4!\) ways. There are five gaps for two separated reds.

\[\begin{aligned}\text{separated}&=4!\binom52=240,\\\text{adjacent}&=5!=120.\end{aligned}\]

The counts sum to \(360=\frac{6!}{2!}\), the total number of patterns.

examples.title: A pair and a single need different gaps
examples.question: Arrange three different ordinary counters and three identical red counters. Count no adjacent reds, exactly one red pair with the third red separate, and all three reds together.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\text{no pair}&=3!\binom43=24,\\\text{one pair}&=3!\times4\times3=72,\\\text{triple}&=4!=24.\end{aligned}\]

In the middle case choose the pair-gap, then a different single-gap. The three cases total \(120=\frac{6!}{3!}\).

lessons.title: Combinations, composition and named-member restrictions
lessons.summary: Build unordered selections once, using disjoint compositions, complements and explicit membership conditions.
lessons.objective: Build unordered selections once, using disjoint compositions, complements and explicit membership conditions.
lessons.before: Work with exact integer counts and identify what makes two outcomes different. Probability applications also use the conditional sample space from the preceding chapter. All arrangements here are in a line or in labelled rows; circular arrangements are excluded.
lessons.ideas:
An unordered selection has no internal order

\[{}^nC_r=\binom nr=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}.\]

Each r-subset of distinct objects has r! orders, which explains the division. Choosing people for different named offices is an ordered assignment, not just a subset.

Compose a group from disjoint categories

Multiply category choices for one fixed composition. For at least or at most conditions, sum over all allowed integer compositions or subtract a disjoint complement. Every case must use the required total group size.

Exactly one, not both, and both-or-neither differ

For two named members, split selections into neither, exactly one and both. A rule that they cannot both serve still allows exactly one; an all-or-none rule does not. Named-member conditions should be applied before filling the remaining places.

A construction must have a constant overcount to divide it away

Choosing one person of each category first and then extra people may count a final group a different number of times depending on its composition. Division by one guessed factor cannot repair a variable overcount. Use final compositions instead.
lessons.method:
1. Decide whether order, object identity and group labels matter.
  2. Choose a disjoint case split or a staged construction.
  3. Count each allowed outcome once and restore internal orders if needed.
  4. Check restrictions, impossible cases and any overcounting factor.
  5. For a probability, use the same kind of equally likely outcome in numerator and denominator.
mistakes: Do not multiply an unordered group count by its internal orders.
Include every feasible composition exactly once.
Cannot both serve does not mean both are absent.
A variable overcount cannot be corrected by one constant divisor.

examples.title: A prescribed composition uses a product
examples.question: Choose two engineers from five and three designers from six. Everyone is different and no offices are assigned. How many teams are possible?
examples.solution:
\[\binom52\binom63=10\times20=200.\]

Within-team order is irrelevant. No further factor of 5! is needed.

examples.title: Partition by the number of named members
examples.question: Select three of seven different people including A and B. Count selections containing exactly one of them, both, and neither.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\text{exactly one}&=2\binom52=20,\\\text{both}&=\binom51=5,\\\text{neither}&=\binom53=10.\end{aligned}\]

The three disjoint counts sum to 35=\(\binom73\).

examples.title: At least two specialists has three compositions
examples.question: Choose four people from six specialists and four trainees, with at least two specialists. Count the allowed teams.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}N&=\binom62\binom42+\binom63\binom41\\&\quad+\binom64\binom40\\&=90+80+15=185.\end{aligned}\]

The complement gives the same result: 210−1−24=185. Zero and exactly one specialist are the forbidden compositions.

examples.title: Two similar-sounding restrictions allow different teams
examples.question: Choose four of ten different people including A and B. Count teams if they cannot both serve. Separately count teams if either both serve or neither serves.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\text{cannot both}&=\binom{10}{4}-\binom82\\&=182,\\\text{both or neither}&=\binom82+\binom84\\&=98.\end{aligned}\]

The first condition allows teams containing exactly one of the two names; the second excludes those teams.

lessons.title: Labelled groups, unnamed divisions and rows of seats
lessons.summary: Identify which group swaps create a new allocation, and distinguish numbered positions from group membership.
lessons.objective: Identify which group swaps create a new allocation, and distinguish numbered positions from group membership.
lessons.before: Work with exact integer counts and identify what makes two outcomes different. Probability applications also use the conditional sample space from the preceding chapter. All arrangements here are in a line or in labelled rows; circular arrangements are excluded.
lessons.ideas:
Named groups are distinct destinations

For labelled groups of prescribed sizes a,b,…, with no internal order, choose members successively or use \(\frac{n!}{a!b!\cdots}\). Do not divide for swapping destinations that are actually named.

Only equivalent unnamed groups can be exchanged

For non-empty unnamed groups of equal size, remove the permutations of those group labels. With different prescribed sizes, groups are already distinguished by size. Divide only for equal-size groups, not automatically by the factorial of the total number of groups.

Fixing one person can avoid a symmetry correction

For two unnamed equal-sized teams, identify one team as the team containing a particular person. Choose that person’s teammates and let the rest form the other team. This counts every division exactly once.

Rows and empty seats need their actual labels

In labelled rows of numbered seats, every position is different. After choosing a group for one row, restore the orders within the rows. Empty positions have no personal identities: do not multiply by a factorial of identical empty slots. Adjacency within a row does not cross to the next row.
lessons.method:
1. Decide whether order, object identity and group labels matter.
  2. Choose a disjoint case split or a staged construction.
  3. Count each allowed outcome once and restore internal orders if needed.
  4. Check restrictions, impossible cases and any overcounting factor.
  5. For a probability, use the same kind of equally likely outcome in numerator and denominator.
mistakes: Named destinations must not be swapped away.
Only equal-size unnamed groups share the same label symmetry.
Membership alone does not assign numbered seats.
Identical empty slots are not different passengers.

examples.title: Two unnamed triples have a twofold label symmetry
examples.question: Divide six different people into two teams of three. Count allocations to named teams East and West, then divisions with no team names.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\text{named}&=\binom63=20,\\\text{unnamed}&=\frac{20}{2!}=10.\end{aligned}\]

Alternatively, choose two partners for A: \(\binom52=10\). The other three people form the other team.

examples.title: An unequal third group does not supply another symmetry
examples.question: Nine different people form groups of sizes 4,4,1. Count allocations to named groups of those sizes and divisions without group names.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\text{named}&=\binom94\binom54=630,\\\text{unnamed}&=\frac{630}{2!}=315.\end{aligned}\]

Only the two four-person groups can be exchanged. The singleton is distinguished by its size, so division by \(3!\) would be incorrect.

examples.title: Sharing a row is weaker than adjacency
examples.question: Six different people fill two labelled rows of three numbered seats. Count arrangements with A and B in the same row, with them adjacent, and find the adjacent probability conditional on sharing a row.
examples.solution:
Let S mean same row and J mean adjacent. For S choose the row, place A and B in two distinct seats, then seat the other four people.

\[\begin{aligned}N(S)&=2({}^3P_2)4!=288,\\N(J)&=2\times2\times2\times4!=192,\\\mathrm P(J\mid S)&=\frac{192}{288}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}\]

For J choose the row, the left or right adjacent pair, the order AB or BA, then arrange the others. The two edge positions in a row are not adjacent to each other.

examples.title: Empty positions are indistinguishable gaps
examples.question: A rack has seven positions in a line. Place four different cases, leaving three empty positions. Count all arrangements, those with all empties consecutive, and those with no adjacent empty positions.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\text{all}&={}^7P_4=840,\\\text{empty block}&=5!=120,\\\text{no adjacency}&=4!\binom53=240.\end{aligned}\]

The final two events are not complements when there are three empty positions; a run of two empties is a further possibility.

lessons.title: Mixed constructions and conditional counting probabilities
lessons.summary: Combine choosing and ordering, match physical sample spaces, and handle overlapping restrictions before conditioning.
lessons.objective: Combine choosing and ordering, match physical sample spaces, and handle overlapping restrictions before conditioning.
lessons.before: Work with exact integer counts and identify what makes two outcomes different. Probability applications also use the conditional sample space from the preceding chapter. All arrangements here are in a line or in labelled rows; circular arrangements are excluded.
lessons.ideas:
Choose and then arrange only when both stages matter

If a condition depends on whether a named object was selected, split on that membership first. A single multiplication works only if every permitted selection has the same number of allowed orders.

Visible patterns need not be equally likely

Different physical tiles carrying the same letter can produce the same visible selection. A uniform random physical subset weights each pattern by how many physical subsets realise it. Do not divide by the number of visible patterns unless uniformity over those patterns is stated.

Overlapping adjacency events share arrangements

If E means AB adjacent and F means BC adjacent, their intersection requires B between A and C in a three-person block. It is not two independent pair-blocks. Exactly one needs the intersection removed twice; a union removes it once.

A conditional count has a restricted denominator

\[\mathrm P(E\mid H)=\frac{N(E\cap H)}{N(H)}.\]

This count ratio is valid when the original elementary outcomes are equally likely and N(H)>0. Use physical subsets on both sides, or arrangements on both sides. In paired-member selections, count complete pairs and single representatives from other pairs without accidentally completing another pair.
lessons.method:
1. Decide whether order, object identity and group labels matter.
  2. Choose a disjoint case split or a staged construction.
  3. Count each allowed outcome once and restore internal orders if needed.
  4. Check restrictions, impossible cases and any overcounting factor.
  5. For a probability, use the same kind of equally likely outcome in numerator and denominator.
mistakes: Some selections have different numbers of allowed orders.
A uniform physical subset does not make all visible patterns equiprobable.
Overlapping blocks cannot be counted as disjoint blocks.
A conditional denominator counts the condition, not the whole original space.

examples.title: A selected name changes the available positions
examples.question: Choose four of seven different objects and arrange them in a line. If A is chosen, A must be first. How many arrangements are possible?
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\text{A included}&=\binom63\,3!=120,\\\text{A absent}&={}^6P_4=360,\\\text{total}&=480.\end{aligned}\]

The two cases are disjoint. They do not have the same number of arrangements per chosen subset.

examples.title: Four patterns arise from six physical subsets
examples.question: There are physical tiles A1,A2,B,C, where A1 and A2 both display A. Two tiles are chosen uniformly. List the visible patterns and find the probabilities of at least one A and exactly one A.
examples.solution:
The patterns are AA, AB, AC, BC. Their physical multiplicities are 1,2,2,1, totalling six equally likely subsets.

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(\text{at least one A})&=\frac{5}{6},\\\mathrm P(\text{exactly one A})&=\frac{4}{6}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}\]

The four visible patterns are not equally likely.

examples.title: One person belongs to both adjacency events
examples.question: Six different people include A,B,C. In a uniform random line, E means AB adjacent and F means BC adjacent. Count their intersection and exactly-one event, then find P(E given at least one of E,F).
examples.solution:
Each single event has \(2(5!)=240\) arrangements. Both require ABC or CBA as one block, giving \(2(4!)=48\). Let X mean exactly one of E and F occurs, and let \(H=E\cup F\).

\[\begin{aligned}N(X)&=240+240-2(48)\\&=384,\\N(H)&=240+240-48\\&=432,\\\mathrm P(E\mid H)&=\frac{240}{432}=\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}\]

examples.title: A complete pair leaves singles from different pairs
examples.question: Four pairs of distinct people form a pool of eight. Choose a four-person team. Count teams with exactly one complete pair and with two complete pairs; find the probability of exactly one given at least one complete pair.
examples.solution:
Let E mean exactly one complete pair and H mean at least one complete pair.

\[\begin{aligned}N(E)&=4\binom32\,2^2=48,\\N(\text{two pairs})&=\binom42=6,\\\mathrm P(E\mid H)&=\frac{48}{54}=\frac{8}{9}.\end{aligned}\]

The remaining two members in the first case come from different remaining pairs. The 16 teams with no complete pair complete the total 70=\(\binom84\).

questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

A 3-digit number is formed using only the digits 0 to 6. A number cannot begin with 0.

  1. Find the number of different numbers that can be formed if no digit is repeated.

    [2]

  2. Find the number of these distinct-digit numbers that are even.

    [3]

  3. Digits may now be repeated. Find the number of even 3-digit numbers whose first digit is at least 2.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:

questions.title: Selecting and ordering short presentations
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

7 students, including Arun and Beth, are available to give presentations. A programme consists of 4 different students listed in the order in which they will speak.

  1. Find the number of possible programmes with no further restrictions.

    [2]

  2. Find the number of programmes which include Arun but do not include Beth.

    [3]

  3. Find the number of programmes which include both Arun and Beth, but in which they do not speak consecutively.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The positions have different roles, so order matters.

\[7\times6\times5\times4=840.\]

(b)

Choose the other 3 students from the 5 students other than Arun and Beth. Then order all 4 selected students, including Arun.

\[\binom{5}{3}4!=240.\]

(c)

Choose the other 2 students in \(\binom{5}{2}\) ways. For any such set there are 4! orders. The forbidden orders treat Arun and Beth as one block, with two internal orders.

\[\binom{5}{2}\bigl(4!-2\times3!\bigr)=120.\]
questions.hint_html: For the final part, first choose the other presenters; then count the allowed orders of the selected group.

Correct total.
Chooses the remaining students with both named students removed from the pool.
Orders the whole selected group.
Correct count.
Chooses the unlabelled remainder of the selected group.

Correct allowed programme count.

    [3]

Arrange the 5 blue displays in 5! ways. They create 6 gaps, including both end gaps. Choose 3 gaps for the reds and then arrange the different red displays.

Only the 4 internal gaps may now contain red displays.

\[5!\binom{4}{3}3!=2880.\]

(c)

The sample space is the restricted set in part (a), not all unrestricted orders.

\[\frac{2880}{14400}=\frac{1}{5}.\]

questions.title: A specified relative order
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

7 different speakers, including Gia, Hugo and Imani, are placed in a programme. Gia must speak before Hugo, and Hugo before Imani; they need not speak consecutively.

\[4!\binom{5}{3}=240.\]
questions.hint_html: The three named presenters must stay in their prescribed order, so do not multiply by 3! at the end.

marking_criteria.description_html: Accounts for the six relative orders of the named speakers.
Correct programme count.
Orders the other speakers and identifies all gaps.
Chooses three separate gaps.
Does not add an extra 3! when the relative order is fixed.

questions.title: Recovering the size of a group
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

A society has \(n\) members. The number of ordered lists of three different members is 10 times the number of unordered pairs of different members. Two members are named Jaya and Karim.

  1. Find n.

    [3]

  2. Find the number of four-member committees that include exactly one of Jaya and Karim.

    [2]

  3. For each such committee, the included named member speaks first and the other members speak in any order. Find the number of possible programmes.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

An ordered list has \(n(n-1)(n-2)\) possibilities and an unordered pair has \(\frac{n(n-1)}2\). Since lists of three exist, \(n\geq3\).

\[\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{n(n-1)/2}=10\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2(n-2)=10\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=7.\]

(b)

Choose the included named member in two ways. Select the other three members from those who are neither Jaya nor Karim.

\[2\binom{5}{3}=20.\]

(c)

Each committee gives exactly 3! orders for the remaining speakers; the first speaker is already fixed.

\[20\times3!=120.\]
questions.hint_html: Write expressions for the ordered list of three and the unordered pair before simplifying their ratio.

marking_criteria.description_html: Distinguishes an ordered list from an unordered pair.
Forms and simplifies the ratio.
Correct positive integer n.
Chooses exactly one named member and excludes the other.
Correct committee count.
Orders only the three remaining committee members.
Correct programme count.

questions.title: Repeated symbols on a display
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

A display contains 3 symbols A, two symbols B and 3 other symbols, each different from every other symbol, in a row. Copies of the same symbol are indistinguishable.

  1. Find the number of different unrestricted displays.

    [2]

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

There are 8 symbols, with repetitions of multiplicities 3 and 2.

(b)

Combine the A symbols into one object. There are then 6 objects, of which two are identical B symbols. Subtract the displays in which the B symbols also form a block.

\[\frac{6!}{2!}-5!=240.\]

questions.title: Exactly one neighbouring pair
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

Three identical red counters and 4 different numbered counters are arranged in a line.

  1. Find the number of arrangements in which no two red counters are next to each other.

    [3]

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Arrange the numbered counters in 4! ways. Choose three different gaps from the 5 available gaps. The red counters are identical, so there is no extra factor of 3!.

(b)

Choose one of the 5 gaps for the pair RR, then a different one of the remaining 4 gaps for the single R. A gap occupied by RRR is excluded. Each permitted arrangement determines these two gaps uniquely.

\[4!(5)(4)=480.\]

questions.prompt_html:

A row contains two identical A symbols, two identical B symbols and 5 other symbols, C, D, E, F, G, all different. Every A must occur before every B, but other symbols may occur anywhere.

  1. Find the number of possible rows.

    [3]

  2. Find the number of these rows in which the A symbols are not next to each other.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Choose the four positions used by A and B. The condition fills them uniquely as A, A, B, B from left to right. Order the other symbols in the remaining positions.

\[\binom{9}{4}5!=15120.\]

(b)

From part (a), subtract rows with AA as a single block. The positions occupied by this block and the two Bs have fixed relative order AA, B, B. All other symbols remain distinct.

\[\binom{9}{4}5!-\binom{8}{3}5!=8400.\]
questions.hint_html: Choose the positions occupied by A and B. Their relative order is fixed, although other symbols may appear between them.

questions.title: Exactly one repeated pair is consecutive
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

Mixed-topic prerequisite: Probability: conditional sample spaces (syllabus 5.3).

There are two identical P tiles, two identical Q tiles and 3 other tiles with different letters. All 7 tiles are arranged in a line.

  1. Find the number of arrangements in which both the Ps are together and the Qs are together.

    [2]

  2. Find the number of arrangements in which exactly one of the pairs PP and QQ is together.

    [4]

  3. Given that at least one of the two pairs is together in a randomly chosen arrangement, find the probability that exactly one pair is together.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Contract PP and QQ into two different blocks. Together with the other tiles, they form 5 different objects.

\[5!=120.\]

(b)

With only PP required to be together, there are \(6!/2!\) arrangements; the Qs are still identical. The same count applies with the roles reversed. An arrangement with both pairs together belongs to both counts and is not allowed, so subtract it from each.

\[2\left(\frac{6!}{2!}-5!\right)=480.\]

(c)

For at least one adjacency condition, subtract the intersection just once from the sum of the two event counts. Thus the conditional sample space has 600 arrangements.

\[\frac{480}{600}=\frac{4}{5}.\]
questions.hint_html: Subtract the arrangements satisfying both adjacency conditions twice when finding exactly one, not once.

marking_criteria.description_html: Contracts both pairs.
Correct simultaneous count.
Counts the arrangements with each one specified pair together.
Subtracts the intersection twice for exactly one condition.
Correct overlap adjustment.
Correct final count.
Uses the at-least-one union as the conditional denominator.
Correct conditional probability.

questions.title: A balanced working group
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

A club contains 6 designers and 5 programmers. No member belongs to both categories. A working group of five members must include at least two from each category. Mina is one of the designers.

  1. Find the number of possible working groups.

    [3]

  2. Find the number of possible working groups which include Mina.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The admissible compositions are two designers with three programmers, or three designers with two programmers. Add the two disjoint counts.

DesignersProgrammersCalculationNumber
23\(\binom{6}{2}\binom{5}{3}\)150
32\(\binom{6}{3}\binom{5}{2}\)200
\[\text{Total}=350.\]

(b)

Include Mina first. A composition requiring k designers now needs k−1 other designers from the remaining 5. The original quota still refers to the full group, including Mina.

Designers in full groupCalculationNumber
2\(\binom{5}{1}\binom{5}{3}\)50
3\(\binom{5}{2}\binom{5}{2}\)100
\[\text{Total}=150.\]
questions.hint_html: List the possible numbers from each category before evaluating the combinations.

marking_criteria.description_html: Lists both permitted compositions.
Uses a product of combinations for each composition.
Correct total.
Includes Mina and reduces only the designer pool and quota.

questions.title: Exactly one named member
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

There are 6 designers and 5 programmers available for a five-member panel, and no person belongs to both categories. Nadia is a designer and Omar is a programmer. Exactly one of Nadia and Omar must be on the panel.

  1. Find the number of possible panels before any further restriction is imposed.

    [2]

  2. Find the number of these panels which contain at least three designers.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Choose which named person is included, then choose the remaining four people from those who are neither Nadia nor Omar.

\[2\binom{9}{4}=252.\]

(b)

Separate the two choices of named member. In every row, choose the unnamed designers from 5 and the unnamed programmers from 4. The counts refer to full panel compositions.

Named memberDesignersProgrammersCount
Nadia3260
Nadia4140
Nadia505
Omar3240
Omar415

For example, the row including Nadia with three designers is \(\binom{5}{2}\binom{4}{2}\), whereas including Omar with three designers gives \(\binom{5}{3}\binom{4}{1}\).

\[\text{Total}=150.\]
questions.hint_html: The case including the named designer has a different remaining quota from the case including the named programmer.

questions.title: A fixed composition and a chair
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

A project panel consists of two designers, two programmers and one tester. There are 5 designers, 4 programmers and 3 testers, all different people, with no overlap between categories. Designer A and programmer B will not both serve on the panel.

  1. Find the number of panels before applying the restriction involving A and B.

    [2]

  2. Find the number of panels which satisfy the restriction.

    [3]

  3. One of the selected designers is appointed chair. Find the number of permitted panels with an appointed chair.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Choose independently within each of the three categories.

\[\binom{5}{2}\binom{4}{2}\binom{3}{1}=180.\]

(b)

A forbidden panel contains A and B, one other designer, one other programmer and one tester. Subtract these panels from part (a).

\[180-(4)(3)(3)=144.\]

(c)

Every permitted panel has exactly two designers and so gives exactly two choices of chair. These are different appointments even if the panel membership is the same.

\[2\times144=288.\]
questions.hint_html: Appointing a chair is an extra choice only after the selected people have been fixed.

questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

A club has 7 senior and 5 junior members. Three particular senior members have agreed that either all three or none of them will serve on a six-member committee.

If all three serve, choose three more members from everyone else. If none serves, all six must be chosen from everyone else. The two cases are disjoint.

\[\left(\binom{4}{1}+\binom{4}{4}\right)\binom{5}{2}=50.\]

questions.title: Why a tempting count overcounts
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

A student chooses five different workshops from 5 art workshops, 4 coding workshops and 3 music workshops. Each workshop belongs to exactly one category. At least one workshop from each category must be chosen.

  1. Find the number of possible selections.

    [4]

  2. A student instead chooses one workshop from each category, and then chooses any two of the remaining workshops. Explain why this does not give a valid count of distinct selections.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(590\).

(b)

It counts the same final selection more than once, and not by a constant factor.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The category counts are a permutation of (3,1,1) or (2,2,1). Enumerate these six distinct compositions, then add their counts.

ArtCodingMusicCalculationNumber
113\(\binom{5}{1}\binom{4}{1}\binom{3}{3}\)20
122\(\binom{5}{1}\binom{4}{2}\binom{3}{2}\)90
131\(\binom{5}{1}\binom{4}{3}\binom{3}{1}\)60
212\(\binom{5}{2}\binom{4}{1}\binom{3}{2}\)120
221\(\binom{5}{2}\binom{4}{2}\binom{3}{1}\)180
311\(\binom{5}{3}\binom{4}{1}\binom{3}{1}\)120
\[\text{Total}=590.\]

(b)

For a fixed final selection with category counts (3,1,1), any of the three workshops in the first category could have been the initially chosen one, so that selection is counted three times. For counts (2,2,1), there are 2×2×1=4 choices of the initially selected representatives, so that selection is counted four times. A single division cannot correct both multiplicities.

The tempting product would be \(5\times4\times3\times\binom{9}{2}=2160\), not the number of distinct selections.

questions.title: Named groups and unnamed groups
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

8 different volunteers are divided into three groups of sizes 3, 3 and 2.

  1. The groups work at the named stations A, B and C, with 3 volunteers at A, 3 at B and 2 at C. Find the number of allocations.

    [3]

  2. Instead, the volunteers are divided into three groups with no names or assigned tasks. Only group membership matters. Find the number of divisions.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Choose the volunteers for A, then B from those remaining. The last volunteers go to C. A and B are named stations, so exchanging their complete groups gives a different allocation.

\[\binom{8}{3}\binom{5}{3}=560.\]

(b)

The two groups of size 3 can be exchanged without changing this division, while the group of size 2 is identified by its different size. Every unnamed division occurs exactly twice in part (a), not six times.

\[\frac{560}{2!}=280.\]
questions.hint_html: Two groups of the same size are interchangeable only when the problem says that the groups are not named.

marking_criteria.description_html: Allocates to the first named station.
Allocates to the next named station from the remainder.
Correct labelled count without division by 2!.
Identifies only the equal-size groups as interchangeable.
Correct division count.

questions.title: Two teams without labels
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

8 different players, including A and B, are divided into two teams of 4. The teams have no labels; exchanging the two complete teams does not give a new division.

  1. Find the number of divisions with no further restrictions.

    [2]

  2. Find the number of divisions in which A and B are in the same team.

    [2]

  3. Find the number of divisions in which A and B are in different teams.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Choosing one team determines the other, but every division is counted twice according to which team is chosen first.

\[\frac{\binom{8}{4}}{2}=35.\]

(b)

The team containing both A and B is uniquely identified. Choose its other 2 members; the remaining team is forced. Do not divide by two again.

\[\binom{6}{2}=15.\]

(c)

Identify the team containing A. Its other 3 members are chosen from the 6 players other than A and B; B automatically belongs to the other team.

\[\binom{6}{3}=20.\]

As a check, the counts in parts (b) and (c) sum to 35.
questions.hint_html: To count teams containing A, use A to identify that team. A second division by 2 is then unnecessary.

marking_criteria.description_html: Chooses one team and recognises twofold counting.
Correct unrestricted division count.
Uses the named pair to identify their team.
Correct count without an extra symmetry division.
Identifies the A team while excluding B.
Correct count and no unnecessary division by two.

questions.title: Keeping categories together when splitting a set
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

Mixed-topic prerequisite: Probability: conditional sample spaces (syllabus 5.3).

There are 3 red, 2 blue and 4 green objects, all physically distinct. A subset of 4 objects is chosen uniformly at random for box A; all remaining objects go into box B.

  1. Find the probability that all red objects are in box A.

    [2]

  2. Find the probability that all red objects are in one box and all blue objects are in the other box.

    [4]

  3. Given that all red objects are in the same box, find the probability that all blue objects are in the other box.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Fix all red objects in A, then choose its remaining 1 objects from the 6 non-red objects.

\[\frac{\binom{6}{1}}{\binom{9}{4}}=\frac{1}{21}.\]

(b)

Either A contains every red object and no blue object, or A contains every blue object and no red object. Fill the remaining places of A with green objects. The two cases are disjoint.

\[\frac{\binom{4}{1}+\binom{4}{2}}{\binom{9}{4}}=\frac{5}{63}.\]

(c)

The condition permits all reds in A or all reds in B. The number of permitted subsets for A is \(\binom{6}{1}+\binom{6}{4}\). Retain the numerator from part (b).

\[\frac{10}{21}=\frac{10}{21}.\]
questions.hint_html: The red objects may all be in either group. In the second part, consider both possible groups containing them.

questions.title: Three teams identified by their members
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

9 different students, including A, B and C, are divided into three teams of 3. The teams have no names and have no assigned order.

  1. Find the number of divisions with no further restrictions.

    [2]

  2. Find the number of divisions in which A and B are in the same team.

    [4]

  3. Find the number of divisions in which A, B and C are in three different teams.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

First allocate to three temporarily named teams. Every unnamed division occurs in 3! orders of those temporary names.

\[\frac{9!}{(3!)^3\,3!}=280.\]

questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

From 6 different landscape photographs and 4 different portrait photographs, three landscapes and two portraits are chosen for a row of five labelled display positions. Each photograph belongs to exactly one category.

    [2]

    [4]

Choose three landscape photographs and two portrait photographs independently.

With landscapes at both ends and portraits separated, the category order must be landscape, portrait, landscape, portrait, landscape. There are 3!×2! orders of the selected photographs in that pattern.

questions.title: Two adjacency events sharing a person
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

Mixed-topic prerequisite: Probability: conditional sample spaces (syllabus 5.3).

7 different people, including A, B and C, stand in a line. Let E be the event that A and B are adjacent, and let F be the event that B and C are adjacent.

  1. Find the number of arrangements in which both E and F occur.

    [2]

  2. Find the number of arrangements in which exactly one of E and F occurs.

    [3]

  3. Given that at least one of E and F occurs in a uniformly chosen arrangement, find the probability that E occurs.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

B must be between A and C, giving the blocks ABC and CBA. Contract the appropriate block; it sits alongside the other 4 people.

\[2\times5!=240.\]

(b)

Each single adjacency event has \(2\times6!\) arrangements. Add the two event counts and remove the intersection twice, because it satisfies neither of the exactly-one cases.

\[4\times6!-4\times5!=2400.\]

(c)

The union includes the intersection once, so its count is \(4\times6!-2\times5!\). The favourable arrangements for E include those in the intersection.

\[\mathrm P(E\mid E\cup F)=\frac{1440}{2640}=\frac{6}{11}.\]
questions.hint_html: If B is next to both A and C, the three-person block is ABC or CBA; there are not four internal orders.

Subtracts the shared intersection twice.
Correct exactly-one count.

questions.title: Recovering membership from selection counts
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

A society contains \(n\) members, including P and Q, where \(n\geq5\). The number of three-member groups containing neither P nor Q is \(2\) times the number containing both P and Q.

  1. Find n.

    [4]

  2. Find the number of three-member groups containing exactly one of P and Q.

    [2]

  3. A four-member committee contains exactly one of P and Q. A chair is appointed from the other three members. Find the number of such committees with an appointed chair.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

There are \(n-2\) groups containing both P and Q, since only one other member is chosen. There are \(\binom{n-2}{3}\) groups containing neither.

\[\frac{(n-2)(n-3)(n-4)}{6}=2(n-2).\]

Cancel the positive factor \(n-2\) and solve the resulting quadratic:

\[(n-3)(n-4)=12,\qquad n(n-7)=0.\]

The root 0 is rejected because \(n\) is at least 5. Hence \(n=7\).

(b)

Choose the included named member in two ways, and the other two group members from the remaining 5.

\[2\binom{5}{2}=20.\]

(c)

Choose the included named member, select three other members, then choose one of those three as chair. The named member is not eligible for this role.

\[2\binom{5}{3}\times3=60.\]
questions.hint_html: Count the three-person groups containing both named members and those containing neither before cancelling common factors.

Uses their ratio and cancels a non-zero factor.
Solves the quadratic and tests the permitted domain.
Correct integer n.
Distinguishes exactly one from at least one.
Correct selection count.
Counts four-member committees with exactly one named member.
Restricts the chair to the other three members.
Correct appointed-committee count.

Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

A society contains \(n\) members, including P and Q, where \(n\geq5\). The number of three-member groups containing neither P nor Q is \(5\) times the number containing both P and Q.

    [2]

(b)

\[2\binom{7}{2}=42.\]

(c)

Choose the included named member, select three other members, then choose one of those three as chair. The named member is not eligible for this role.

\[2\binom{7}{3}\times3=210.\]

questions.title: Exactly two complete pairs
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

Mixed-topic prerequisite: Probability: conditional sample spaces (syllabus 5.3).

A club consists of 5 pairs of twins. All 10 members are different, and each member belongs to exactly one pair. A team of six is selected.

  1. Find the number of teams containing exactly two complete pairs of twins.

    [4]

  2. A team is chosen uniformly at random. Find the probability that it contains at least two complete pairs.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Choose the two complete pairs. The two remaining team members must come singly from two different remaining pairs. Choose those two pairs, then one of the two twins in each.

(b)

Besides the teams in part (a), a team can consist of three complete pairs. There are \(\binom{5}{3}\)=10 such teams. The cases are disjoint.

\[\frac{120+10}{\binom{10}{6}}=\frac{13}{21}.\]

questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

Mixed-topic prerequisite: Probability: conditional sample spaces (syllabus 5.3).

10 different students occupy two labelled rows of 5 numbered seats. Three particular friends, A, B and C, must sit in the same row. All seats are occupied; adjacency is considered within a row only.

  1. Find the number of arrangements satisfying this condition.

    [3]

  2. Find the number of these arrangements in which none of the three friends sit next to another of the three.

    [4]

  3. An arrangement is chosen uniformly from those satisfying the same-row condition. Find the probability that no two of the three friends are adjacent.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Choose the common row in two ways, choose three seats in it, assign A, B and C to those seats and arrange everyone else.

\[2\binom{5}{3}3!7!=604800.\]

(b)

For three non-adjacent positions \(i<j<k\), subtract 0, 1 and 2 respectively. The resulting three positions form an arbitrary increasing triple among 3 positions. This gives \(\binom{3}{3}\) allowed seat sets.

\[2\binom{3}{3}3!7!=60480.\]

(c)

Divide the count in part (b) by the count in part (a). The row and person-order factors cancel.

\[\frac{\binom{3}{3}}{\binom{5}{3}}=\frac{1}{10}.\]

questions.title: Three friends in the same row
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

Mixed-topic prerequisite: Probability: conditional sample spaces (syllabus 5.3).

14 different students occupy two labelled rows of 7 numbered seats. Three particular friends, A, B and C, must sit in the same row. All seats are occupied; adjacency is considered within a row only.

  1. Find the number of arrangements satisfying this condition.

    [3]

  2. Find the number of these arrangements in which none of the three friends sit next to another of the three.

    [4]

  3. An arrangement is chosen uniformly from those satisfying the same-row condition. Find the probability that no two of the three friends are adjacent.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Choose the common row in two ways, choose three seats in it, assign A, B and C to those seats and arrange everyone else.

\[2\binom{7}{3}3!11!=16765056000.\]

(b)

For three non-adjacent positions \(i<j<k\), subtract 0, 1 and 2 respectively. The resulting three positions form an arbitrary increasing triple among 5 positions. This gives \(\binom{5}{3}\) allowed seat sets.

\[2\binom{5}{3}3!11!=4790016000.\]

(c)

Divide the count in part (b) by the count in part (a). The row and person-order factors cancel.

\[\frac{\binom{5}{3}}{\binom{7}{3}}=\frac{2}{7}.\]
questions.hint_html: Once the common row is chosen, count triples of non-adjacent positions in that row. The remaining people fill every other seat.

questions.title: A minimum separation at a display
questions.prompt_html:
Counts are exact integers. Distinguish physical objects, identical patterns and group labels. For probabilities, match the stated equally likely and conditional sample space.

Mixed-topic prerequisite: Probability: conditional sample spaces (syllabus 5.3).

A display contains 8 different ordinary exhibits and three different special exhibits. All 11 exhibits are placed in one line. An ordinary exhibit must be at each end.

  1. Find the number of arrangements in which no two special exhibits are adjacent.

    [3]

  2. Find the number of arrangements in which there are at least two ordinary exhibits between any two special exhibits.

    [4]

  3. An arrangement is chosen uniformly from those in part (a). Find the probability that it also satisfies the condition in part (b).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Arrange the 8 ordinary exhibits first. Only the 7 internal gaps may contain a special exhibit, because both end exhibits must be ordinary. Choose three different gaps and order the three special exhibits.

\[8!\binom{7}{3}3!=8467200.\]

(b)

Number the internal gaps from 1 to 7. If the chosen gaps are \(i<j<k\), adjacent gaps would leave only one ordinary exhibit between special exhibits. Hence \(j\geq i+2\) and \(k\geq j+2\).

The mapping \((i,j,k)\mapsto(i,j-1,k-2)\) is a one-to-one correspondence with increasing triples from 1 to 5. Thus there are \(\binom{5}{3}\) allowed gap triples. This argument establishes the count without assuming a formula for separated selections.

\[8!\binom{5}{3}3!=2419200.\]

(c)

Use the allowed arrangements in part (a) as the conditional sample space. The identity-order factors cancel, but the different gap counts remain.

\[\frac{\binom{5}{3}}{\binom{7}{3}}=\frac{2}{7}.\]
questions.hint_html: Use the gaps between the ordinary objects. Requiring two ordinary objects between special ones means the chosen gaps cannot be consecutive.
